item.content:encoded:
Trump proposes tariffs on 14 partners; China rate could reach 40%

Category: Business

The Trump administration proposed new tariffs on imports from 14 major trading partners, citing excess manufacturing capacity after a U.S. Supreme Court ruling in February struck down much of President Donald Trump’s earlier broad-based tariff program. U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the countries’ manufacturing policies burden or restrict U.S. commerce; the proposed duties would rely on a different legal authority, Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 [3][4]. A separate proposal targets Brazilian sugar and finished aircraft, including a 10% duty on aircraft [4]. China faces a proposed 20% rate that Washington says could rise to 40% if Beijing does not adequately engage. Vietnam could face up to 35%, while several other proposed rates are subject to caps or reductions tied to trade agreements [11][3]. The proposals drew objections from China, Japan, Singapore, the European Union and Brazil, among others [3][4]. The duties are not final: affected parties can submit comments, and a hearing is scheduled for Jan. 25. Final tariffs are expected as early as February or March. Economist Stephen Brown of Capital Economics said the new measures would largely replace earlier tariffs but could still keep core goods inflation firm into next year [6][15][12].

Primary Source: View original article

Read more: Full article on Kite Static

China will closely monitor developments and reserves the right to take necessary measures to firmly defend its legitimate rights and interests.

— He Yadong, spokesperson for China’s Ministry of Commerce (Channel News Asia)

Key Points

  • China exemptions: The U.S. proposal exempts about $30 billion of Chinese goods covered by reciprocal tariff cuts [15][16].
  • Singapore trade: Singapore says the U.S. has run a trade surplus with the city-state for more than 20 years; under their free-trade agreement, Singapore imposes no tariffs on U.S. goods [11].
  • Investigation scope: The U.S. probe covered sectors including steel, aluminum, automobiles, batteries, chemicals, electronics, semiconductors, solar modules and shipbuilding [8].
  • Brazilian exports: Brazil said it had negotiated in good faith with Washington on the Section 301 matter for more than a year before objecting to the new proposal [4].
  • Market response: After the announcement, the Nasdaq Composite fell 0.62% and the S&P 500 slipped 0.25%; WisdomTree research director Aneeka Gupta cited renewed uncertainty over technology investment plans [27].

Perspectives

Trump administration: Greer said the measures are intended to level the playing field for U.S. workers and respond to market-distorting practices that he said weaken U.S. manufacturing [4].

Sources: TIME

China’s Ministry of Commerce: Spokesperson He Yadong argued the tariffs would disrupt supply chains, raise inflation and harm businesses and consumers, and called for negotiations rather than unilateral measures [15].

Sources: South China Morning Post

Brazilian government: Brasília said it would continue negotiating but would not rule out retaliatory measures against what it called an unacceptable unilateral action [6].

Sources: The Guardian

Timeline

  • October 2025: Trump and Xi agreed to a trade ceasefire [25]
  • February 2026: Supreme Court struck down much of Trump’s broad tariff program [10]
  • March 2026: USTR launched its excess-capacity investigation under Section 301 [21]
  • 25 November 2026: Administration announced proposed tariffs on 14 trading partners [4]
  • 10 January 2027: Current U.S.-China trade truce is scheduled to expire [3]
  • 25 January 2027: Public hearing on proposed tariffs is scheduled [6]

Technical Details

  • Section 301 authority: The administration is using Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which allows the U.S. Trade Representative to investigate foreign trade practices and propose responsive duties; the proposals still face public consultation and hearings [4][10].
  • Tariff stacking: Some Chinese imports may face the proposed duties in addition to existing Section 301 tariffs from 2018, while other tariff exclusions differ by product and country; this can make the total duty higher than the headline rate [15].

Industry Impact

  • Singapore exporters: If the maximum rate is imposed, about one-third of Singapore’s direct exports—S$9.4 billion—would be affected, and the effective tariff on those exports could reach 10.3% from 7.8% [11].
  • Aircraft manufacturing: Brazil’s largest aircraft maker, Embraer, could be affected by the proposed additional 10% U.S. tariff on finished aircraft from Brazil [8][6].

Historical Background

In October 2025, President Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed to a trade ceasefire, which was later extended and is due to expire on Jan. 10, 2027 [25][3]. During an earlier escalation, U.S. and Chinese tariffs briefly reached 145%, before the two sides negotiated a truce [25].

Business Angle

  • Trade agreements could change competitive positions: proposed rates for India and Vietnam could fall from 25% to 17% and from as much as 35% to 20%, respectively, if negotiations produce deals [11].
  • Retaliation remains a material risk for exporters; the American Soybean Association warned that renewed counter-tariffs could burden farmers already near break-even after prior losses [19].

International Reactions

  • 🇨🇳 China: Beijing rejected the U.S. overcapacity rationale and reserved the right to respond, while urging Washington to resume dialogue [15].
  • 🇪🇺 European Union: The European Commission rejected the claim that Europe is a source of structural overcapacity and said it expected Washington to honor the existing trade deal [6].
  • 🇯🇵 Japan: Tokyo protested the proposal; Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara denied that Japan has structural excess manufacturing capacity [3].

Q&A

Q: Why does the proposal scrutinize Southeast Asian economies as well as China?

A: A European Council on Foreign Relations policy fellow said Washington is concerned that Chinese goods pass through regional economies before reaching the U.S. market, and that the tariffs are intended to make it harder for places such as Vietnam to serve as intermediaries [4].

item.title: Denny’s restores Nvidia founder plaque as Huang returns to CEO role
item.author: Kite Feed Generator (Business / Corporate Governance)
item.description: Denny’s publicly welcomed Jensen Huang back as Nvidia’s chief executive and said it had restored a plaque marking the San Jose diner booth where Huang and co-founders Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem discussed starting the chipmaker [2][3]. The restaurant chain said it learned the plaque had been removed on Nov. 13, one day after Huang resigned, and put it back shortly afterward. It has not said who removed it or why [1][8]. Nvidia’s board reinstated Huang on Nov. 23, 11 days after accepting his resignation following reports of an affair with a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, a customer suspected of links to Chinese intelligence. Huang acknowledged infidelity; Nvidia’s independent board review is continuing [14][16][4]. The board said it considered input from senior U.S. government officials, while President Donald Trump has said he helped secure Huang’s return [14][11]. Denny’s posted its renewed tribute on Nov. 25. The endorsement drew online mockery and criticism. Huang’s reinstatement also renewed questions about Nvidia’s succession planning, board independence and oversight of export-control compliance [3][14][16].
item.content:encoded:
Denny’s restores Nvidia founder plaque as Huang returns to CEO role

Category: Business

Denny’s publicly welcomed Jensen Huang back as Nvidia’s chief executive and said it had restored a plaque marking the San Jose diner booth where Huang and co-founders Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem discussed starting the chipmaker [2][3]. The restaurant chain said it learned the plaque had been removed on Nov. 13, one day after Huang resigned, and put it back shortly afterward. It has not said who removed it or why [1][8]. Nvidia’s board reinstated Huang on Nov. 23, 11 days after accepting his resignation following reports of an affair with a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, a customer suspected of links to Chinese intelligence. Huang acknowledged infidelity; Nvidia’s independent board review is continuing [14][16][4]. The board said it considered input from senior U.S. government officials, while President Donald Trump has said he helped secure Huang’s return [14][11]. Denny’s posted its renewed tribute on Nov. 25. The endorsement drew online mockery and criticism. Huang’s reinstatement also renewed questions about Nvidia’s succession planning, board independence and oversight of export-control compliance [3][14][16].

Primary Source: View original article

Read more: Full article on Kite Static

a better CEO the second time around

— Jensen Huang, Nvidia chief executive (Financial Times)

Key Points

  • Online response: Business Insider reported that Denny’s post had drawn more than 3.9 million views on X, with commenters divided between jokes and criticism of the chain’s support for Huang [3].
  • Board scrutiny: Four Nvidia directors joined the board in 1993 or 1997, and governance experts questioned whether long-serving directors can remain independent [14].
  • Compliance changes: Nvidia’s board said it would appoint a chief compliance officer and created a committee to oversee national security and export controls [16].
  • Credit risk: S&P Global Ratings warned it could cut Nvidia’s AA issuer rating by one notch if the company does not address governance deficiencies [16].
  • Leadership structure: Huang defended a flat structure in which dozens of senior executives report directly to him [16].

Perspectives

Denny’s: The chain says Huang’s personal history with it began when he worked there as a teenager, and that Nvidia’s origin story is part of Denny’s history worth preserving [1][2].

Sources: The Seattle Times

Kathleen Day, Johns Hopkins Carey Business School lecturer: Day said shareholders should demand a new board, arguing directors must represent shareholders rather than the chief executive [14].

Sources: NBC Bay Area

Timeline

  • 10 November 2026: Denny’s contacted Nvidia communications to affirm their shared history [2]
  • 12 November 2026: Nvidia’s board accepted Huang’s resignation [14][8]
  • 13 November 2026: Denny’s learned the commemorative plaque had been removed [1][2]
  • 23 November 2026: Nvidia’s board unanimously reinstated Huang as chief executive [10][14]
  • 25 November 2026: Denny’s posted its public welcome to Huang on social media [2][3]

Historical Background

Denny’s installed the plaque in 2023, describing the booth as the birthplace of a $1 trillion company; Nvidia was founded in 1993 [2][13].

Q&A

Q: What part of Nvidia’s business practices is under additional scrutiny?

A: The California Department of Justice said it was asking Nvidia whether advanced chips or confidential information may have reached China and whether the company misled investors or the public [14].
